Foundations

Big data, its story, and the data itself

Big data primer: the 5 V's

📦Volume

How much. From about 2 ZB a year in 2010 to roughly 175–200 ZB in 2025 (IDC estimates).

How do we store it?

⚡Velocity

How fast. The world creates around 0.4–0.5 ZB per day; a growing share is real-time.

How fast must we process it?

🧩Variety

How many shapes: tables, JSON, logs, images, audio… and now embeddings for AI.

How do we handle every format?

🔍Veracity

How trustworthy. More important than ever: AI amplifies whatever errors are in the data.

Can we trust it?

💶Value

Why bother. Data is an asset; big data is a must-have capability in every industry.

What decision does it improve?

Takeaway: big data is the result of the evolution of data, technology and BI. It's not about size alone, but about what the old tools couldn't handle.
You saw it in the labs: volume (605,765 flights), velocity (Binance ticks every second), variety (CSV, JSON, WebSocket messages) and veracity ("NA" hiding nulls).

From two Google papers to lakehouses and AI

Big data today (2026): five shifts

☁️ From clusters to the cloud

Managed services instead of Hadoop clusters. Q2 2026: AWS 28%, Azure 20%, Google Cloud 15% of cloud infrastructure (Synergy Research).

AWSGoogle Cloud
🧱 Storage and compute apart

Data sits cheaply in object storage (S3, MinIO); engines scale up and down on demand. That's why our labs read s3a://.

S3MinIO
🏠 Lakehouse & open table formats

Iceberg, Delta Lake and Hudi add ACID transactions, schema evolution and time travel to files in the lake.

Delta LakeParquetDatabricksSnowflake
⚡ Streaming first

Real-time pipelines are mainstream: Kafka 4 (no ZooKeeper), Flink 2, Spark Structured Streaming.

KafkaFlinkSpark
🧭 Data mesh & data products

Domain teams own and publish their data as documented, governed products.

🤖 Big data meets AI

LLMs, RAG with embeddings and vector search… and AI-ready data as the deciding factor: Gartner expects 60% of AI projects without it to be abandoned through 2026.

Data & files: structure decides the tools

One day of TfL bike data, 230,112 rows (lecture 6.2)
JSON46.1 MB
CSV22.4 MB
CSV + gzip5.7 MB
Parquet0.9 MB
  • Text formats (CSV, JSON) are easy to read and to ingest: land raw data as it arrives.
  • Storage formats (Parquet, ORC, Avro) are binary and built for analytics: columnar, compressed, with the schema inside.
  • Parquet was 24× smaller than CSV and read 2 columns in 0.01 s vs 0.24 s for the whole CSV.
ParquetpandasDuckDBSpark

Ingestion

Capture the data and bring it into the storage layer

Data ingestion: the toughest part

Why so hard? Many sources, variable speed and variety, unreliable networks, credentials, formats that change.
No single tool: we often need several technologies depending on the source and the latency required.
Start from requirements: latency, source type, volume, platform, team skills, cost. Then pick NiFi, Airflow, CDC, managed connectors…

Apache NiFi: data flows you can see

An easy-to-use, powerful and reliable system to process and distribute data: it addresses the challenges of enterprise data ingestion at scale.

FlowFilea piece of data: content + attributes (filename, ${now()}…)
Processordoes one job: InvokeHTTP, SplitJson, PutHDFS, PutS3Object, PublishKafka
Connectiona queue between processors, with back pressure
Process Groupa reusable sub-flow; exported as a JSON flow definition
Controller Serviceshared config: credentials, SSL, WebSocket client
Provenancethe full history of every FlowFile
Lesson from the labs: sensitive values are not exported with a flow: after every import, add the keys again in the controller services.
3

Storage

A batch store and a streaming store

Two stores, two jobs

🗂️Batch storage · file based

Volume + variety. Maybe the most important one, because it stores all the data. It must be carefully designed to enforce security, data quality and governance.

HDFSMinIOAmazon S3ParquetDelta Lake
🌊Streaming storage · event based

Velocity + variety. Eases and speeds up real-time processing. Events that enter this way are also stored in the batch store.

Apache KafkaPulsar
Almost every big data solution needs both. In lab 8.2 one NiFi flow fed both: a file per minute to MinIO and every tick to Kafka.

A data lake you can navigate

Pattern from the labs: /<layer>/<source>/<dataset>/…. Names, not tools, make a lake navigable; without them it becomes a data swamp.

HDFS and Kafka in one picture each

HDFS · big files, split and replicated
Kafka · an ordered, replayable log of events

Processing

From MapReduce to Spark DataFrames and SQL

Processing: the right engine for each job

TypeGoalTechnologies (2026)
🧺 Batchprocess large, finished datasetsSparkMapReduce (legacy)
⚡ Streamreact to events within secondsFlink 2Structured StreamingKafka Streams
🔄 ETL / ELTextract, clean, reshape, loadPySparkLakeflow dbt
🧾 SQLquery the lake with SQLHive 4TrinoSpark SQLDuckDBBigQuerySnowflake
🕸️ Graphrelationships, paths, communitiesGraphFrames · Neo4j
🧠 ML / AItrain models, embeddings, RAGMLlibDatabricks vector search
🗓️ Workflow managersschedule and chain all of the aboveAirflow 3 Kestra (in OSBDET)
Takeaway: Apache Spark and Apache Flink are the most versatile processing technologies today; Apache Hive is one of the oldest and most influential for SQL on big data.

Hadoop and MapReduce: move the code, not the data

  • Key idea: drive computation to where the data is stored.
  • Still maintained (3.5 current, OSBDET ships 3.4), but considered legacy: its ideas live on everywhere.
Lab 10.1 · movies per genre with Hadoop Streaming

Every MapReduce job is map → shuffle → reduce, reading from and writing to disk at each step. Simple, robust… and slow for anything iterative. That's what Spark fixed.

Apache Spark: one engine, many workloads

The Spark Data API: two levels, two kinds of operation

Use the high-level API by default: Catalyst optimises it; RDDs are for the few things DataFrames can't express.
Driver memory: collect() and toPandas() bring everything to the driver: limit() first.

What Spark really did: jobs, stages, shuffles

  • Job = one action. Stage = the work between two shuffles. Task = one stage on one partition.
  • "skipped" stages: Spark reused shuffle files it already had.
  • The UI is your best debugging friend: slow? Look for big shuffles and skewed tasks.

One question, four ways: movies per genre

MapReduce
# mapper.py
for line in sys.stdin:
  g = line.rsplit(",", 1)[-1]
  for x in g.strip().split("|"):
    print(f"{x}\t1")
# reducer.py: sum the 1s
# per sorted key
# + hadoop jar … streaming
#   -mapper -reducer
2 scripts · disk between steps
RDD
(sc.textFile("movies.csv")
   .filter(lambda l: not
       l.startswith("movieId"))
   .flatMap(lambda l:
       [(g, 1) for g in
        l.rsplit(",",1)[-1]
         .split("|")])
   .reduceByKey(lambda a, b:
       a + b))
functional · in memory · you parse
DataFrame
(spark.read
   .option("header", True)
   .csv("movies.csv")
   .select(F.explode(
       F.split("genres",
               r"\|"))
     .alias("genre"))
   .groupBy("genre")
   .count()
   .orderBy(F.desc("count")))
declarative · optimised · CSV parsed for you
SQL
movies_df.createOrReplace\
  TempView("movies")

spark.sql("""
SELECT genre, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM movies
LATERAL VIEW explode(
  split(genres, '[|]'))
  t AS genre
GROUP BY genre
ORDER BY n DESC""")
the same plan as the DataFrame
Drama 4361 · Comedy 3756 · Thriller 1894 · Action 1828 …
# all four ways agree

From 2 scripts and a shell command to 1 line of SQL: twenty years of big data progress on one slide. Results verified on MovieLens ml-latest-small (9,742 movies, 20 genres).

SQL and DataFrames: one engine

bikepoint_df.createOrReplaceTempView("BikePoints")

spark_session.sql("""
  SELECT id, commonName,
         MIN(CAST(value AS INT)) AS min_bikes,
         MAX(CAST(value AS INT)) AS max_bikes,
         ROUND(AVG(CAST(value AS INT)), 2) AS avg_bikes
  FROM BikePoints WHERE key = 'NbBikes'
  GROUP BY id, commonName""")       # → a DataFrame
  • A temporary view is just a name in the session's catalog for a DataFrame's plan.
  • sql() returns a DataFrame: keep chaining DataFrame methods, or register it again.
  • explain() showed the same physical plan for SQL and the DataFrame API (lab 18.1).
Choose the API that reads best for each step. Your SQL skills transfer directly to big data.

Every number on this slide was computed in class, on real data, with the tools of the course. That's the point: you can now check claims like these yourself.

Ten traps we learnt to avoid

1
Numbers stored as textmin/max go alphabetical: "13" < "9". Cast before aggregating.
2
Missing values in disguise"NA" isn't null: null checks said 0. Use .option("nullValue", "NA").
3
inferSchema reads twiceFine for labs; declare a schema for big data.
4
Commas inside quotes"American President, The (1995)" broke naive split(","). Use a CSV reader or rsplit.
5
Everything to the drivercollect()/toPandas() on big data crash the driver: limit() first.
6
Only one table showsJupyter displays the last expression: wrap each in display().
7
"% of what?"Percentages that summed to 96.92%: pick one denominator and say it.
8
Tiny groups win rankings9 flights at Adak → 22%. Set a minimum volume.
9
Credentials go missing… or leakNiFi doesn't export secrets; Git must never store them.
10
Time is trickyhhmm integers, session time zones, and modified ≠ snapshot time.
Each trap came from a real lab, not a textbook. Most of them show up the same way in SQL, pandas or any cloud platform: the habits transfer.

What's next

The group assignment and the road ahead

Your group assignment: an EDA checklist

  1. Land the data in the lake with a clear name: /<layer>/<source>/<dataset>/ or a bucket per source.
  2. Metadata: schema, size, samples, entities, metrics, dimensions, column groups.
  3. Profile each group: summary(), nulls, distinct values, most and least frequent.
  4. Fix how you read what profiling reveals: types, null markers, odd values.
  5. Answer business questions with clear denominators and minimum volumes.
  6. Tell the story: charts, a few numbers that matter, and what the business should do.
Before you submit, check: types first · min ≤ quartiles ≤ max · parts add up to totals · "% of what" next to every percentage · every table matches its title.
Your reference: lab 17.1 (Flights EDA) shows every step on real data, including the mistakes worth fixing.
